newsitem.title: CANADA: Service seen bidding $45-$48/shr for Loewen.
newsitem.headline: Service seen bidding $45-$48/shr for Loewen.

text.p: Service Corp International, North America's biggest funeral home and cemetery operator, is expected to raise its bid for rival the Loewen Group Inc to US$45 to US$48 a share next week, analysts and institutional investors said Friday.

Loewen, the second biggest in the industry, this week spurned a US$43 a share stock offer from Houston-based Service Corp that valued it at US$2.8 billion. Service Corp's board is scheduled to meet Tuesday and many analysts believe it is likely to launch a formal hostile bid.
"I think that is very realistic," Dean Witter analyst Todd Richter said of a bid in the range of US$45 to US$48. "Up to the high 40s it's a good deal" for Service Corp."
Raymond James analyst Susan Little looked for Service Corp to offer US$46 to US$48 a share. Loewen stock was trading at 40-7/8, down 1/4, while Service Corp was up 1/2 at 30-1/2.
Analysts and investors said a higher bid would intensify pressure on Loewen to negotiate a deal but expected Loewen to continue to resist.
"You've got an entrenched management (at Loewen) that does not want to sell at any price," said Richter.

Until now, Loewen has flatly rejected the idea of being acquired by Service Corp and chief executive Ray Loewen, who holds 15 percent of the company's shares, has said even US$52 a share would not make him feel under any pressure to sell.
This stance has irked some of the company's institutional investors.

"Ray Loewen is blowing smoke when he says they are not for sale at any price...That is an absurdity. When it gets to $50-$52, he is going to be pushed very hard by his shareholders," said one money manager.
One analyst who asked not to be identified said some institutions would not be satisfied with a deal below US$50 and some traders speculated Loewen could fetch US$55 a share.

But some investors remain wary, saying Loewen may manage to block a deal even if the price is attractive to outside shareholders. "The odds of Loewen remaining independent are quite high," said one trader.

Ray Loewen has said that with his shares and those in friendly hands he could likely scuttle a hostile deal because of a British Columbia law requiring the acquiror to win 75 percent of the shares outstanding.
Service Corp is also cautious about potential earnings dilution from the takeover and that will affect its strategy, analysts said.

Service Corp wants to be able to treat the acquisition as a pooling of interests rather than use the purchase accounting method which would require it to amortize the good will and could mean a significant dilution to its earnings.
